claim: Natural killer (NK) cells are innate lymphoid cells that are essential for innate and adaptive immunity.
source: Natural killer (NK) cells are innate lymphoid cells that are essential for innate and adaptive immunity.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about NK cells.

claim: Mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) is critical for NK cell development.
source: Mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) is critical for NK cell development
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The independent roles of mTORC1 or mTORC2 in regulating NK cell development remain unknown.
source: however, the independent roles of mTORC1 or mTORC2 in regulating this process remain unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Ncr1iCre-mediated deletion of Rptor or Rictor in mice results in altered homeostatic NK cellularity.
source: Ncr1iCre-mediated deletion of Rptor or Rictor in mice results in altered homeostatic NK cellularity and impaired development at distinct stages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Ncr1iCre-mediated deletion of Rptor or Rictor in mice results in impaired development at distinct stages.
source: Ncr1iCre-mediated deletion of Rptor or Rictor in mice results in altered homeostatic NK cellularity and impaired development at distinct stages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The transition from the CD27+CD11b− to the CD27+CD11b+ stage is impaired in Rptor cKO mice.
source: The transition from the CD27+CD11b− to the CD27+CD11b+ stage is impaired in Rptor cKO mice
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The terminal maturation from the CD27+CD11b+ to the CD27−CD11b+ stage is compromised in Rictor cKO mice.
source: while, the terminal maturation from the CD27+CD11b+ to the CD27−CD11b+ stage is compromised in Rictor cKO mice.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Raptor-deficiency renders substantial alteration of the gene expression profile including transcription factors governing early NK cell development.
source: Mechanistically, Raptor-deficiency renders substantial alteration of the gene expression profile including transcription factors governing early NK cell development.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: Loss of Rictor causes more restricted transcriptome changes compared to loss of Raptor.
source: Comparatively, loss of Rictor causes more restricted transcriptome changes.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data showing fewer differentially expressed genes in Rictor cKO compared to Rptor cKO (Figure 5A).

claim: The reduced expression of T-bet correlates with the terminal maturation defects in Rictor cKO mice.
source: The reduced expression of T-bet correlates with the terminal maturation defects
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced T-bet expression (Figure 3D) and terminal maturation defects (Figure 2E) in Rictor cKO mice.

claim: The reduced expression of T-bet results from impaired mTORC2-AktS473-FoxO1 signaling.
source: The reduced expression of T-bet correlates with the terminal maturation defects and results from impaired mTORC2-AktS473-FoxO1 signaling.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced AktS473 and FoxO1 phosphorylation (Figure 6B) and enrichment of FoxO1 target genes (Figure 6C) in Rictor cKO mice.

claim: mTORC1 and mTORC2 have divergent roles in NK cell development.
source: Collectively, our results reveal the divergent roles of mTORC1 and mTORC2 in NK cell development.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all experimental data showing distinct developmental defects in Rptor vs Rictor cKO mice.

claim: Humans with NK cell deficiency are more susceptible to viral infection, especially herpesviruses.
source: Humans with NK cell deficiency are more susceptible to viral infection, especially herpesviruses (Orange, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: NK cell adoptive transfer has been explored as promising adjuvant therapy.
source: NK cell adoptive transfer has been explored as promising adjuvant therapy (Curti et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2005; Rubnitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NK cells develop in the bone marrow (BM) and progress through distinct differentiation stages.
source: NK cells develop in the bone marrow (BM) and progress through distinct differentiation stages (Di Santo, 2006).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Expression of IL-15/IL-2 receptor β chain (CD122) defines the commitment of common lymphoid progenitor (CLP) cells to the NK cell lineage.
source: Expression of IL-15/IL-2 receptor β chain (CD122) defines the commitment of common lymphoid progenitor (CLP) cells to the NK cell lineage (Rosmaraki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: NK cell progenitors (NKP) have been refined as Lin−Flt3−CD27+2B4+CD127+CD122+NK1.1− cells.
source: Recently, the cell surface markers-defined NK cell progenitors (NKP) have been refined as Lin−Flt3−CD27+2B4+CD127+CD122+NK1.1− cells (Carotta et al., 2011; Fathman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Committed NKPs differentiate into immature (iNK; Lin−CD122+NK1.1+DX5−) and eventually mature NK cells (mNK; Lin−CD122+NK1.1+DX5+).
source: Committed NKPs differentiate into immature (iNK; Lin−CD122+NK1.1+DX5−) and eventually mature NK cells (mNK; Lin−CD122+NK1.1+DX5+) (Di Santo, 2006; Kim et al., 2002b; Rosmaraki et al., 2001; Williams et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Development of NK cells following NK1.1 expression is further defined into three groups based on CD27 and CD11b expression.
source: Development of NK cells following NK1.1 expression is further defined into three groups based on CD27 and CD11b expression (Hayakawa and Smyth, 2006; Kim et al., 2002b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CD27+CD11b− (CD27 single positive, SP) NK cells differentiate into CD27+CD11b+ (double positive, DP) cells.
source: Adoptive transfer experiments have demonstrated that CD27+CD11b− (CD27 single positive, SP) NK cells differentiate into CD27+CD11b+ (double positive, DP) cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: DP NK cells down-regulate CD27 to mature into CD27−CD11b+ (CD11b SP) cells, the terminally matured NK cell population which expresses KLRG1.
source: DP NK cells down-regulate CD27 to mature into CD27−CD11b+ (CD11b SP) cells, the terminally matured NK cell population which expresses KLRG1 (Chiossone et al., 2009; Huntington et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Eomesodermin (Eomes) and T-bet play critical roles in distinct maturation stages of NK cells.
source: NK cell differentiation is driven by stage-specific transcription factors including Eomesodermin (Eomes) and T-bet which play critical roles in distinct maturation stages of NK cells (Daussy et al., 2014; Gordon et al., 2012; Townsend et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Eomes is essential in driving maturation of CD27 SP to DP NK cells.
source: Genetic knockout models demonstrated that Eomes is essential in driving maturation of CD27 SP to DP NK cells, while T-bet governs the terminal maturation of the DP to CD11b SP NK cells (Gordon et al., 2012; Townsend et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior genetic knockout studies.

claim: T-bet governs the terminal maturation of the DP to CD11b SP NK cells.
source: Genetic knockout models demonstrated that Eomes is essential in driving maturation of CD27 SP to DP NK cells, while T-bet governs the terminal maturation of the DP to CD11b SP NK cells (Gordon et al., 2012; Townsend et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior genetic knockout studies.

claim: mTOR is an evolutionarily conserved serine/threonine kinase that forms two functionally distinct complexes, mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2).
source: mTOR is an evolutionarily conserved serine/threonine kinase that forms two functionally distinct complexes, mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) (Saxton and Sabatini, 2017; Wullschleger et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Raptor and Rictor are the defining components of mTORC1 and mTORC2, respectively.
source: Raptor and Rictor are the defining components of mTORC1 and mTORC2, respectively (Hara et al., 2002; Jacinto et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2002a; Sarbassov et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: mTOR complexes regulate cell growth, proliferation, and metabolism and play an indispensable role in immune cells.
source: These complexes regulate cell growth, proliferation, and metabolism and play an indispensable role in immune cells (Powell et al., 2012; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017; Weichhart et al., 2015; Wullschleger et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The activation of mTORC1 involves the canonical PI3K-PDK1-Akt-TSC1/2-mTORC1 pathway.
source: The activation of mTORC1 involves the canonical PI3K-PDK1-Akt-TSC1/2-mTORC1 pathway (Saxton and Sabatini, 2017; Yang and Guan, 2007).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PtdIns(3,4,5)P3, which is generated by PI3K, has been shown to be critical for mTORC2 activation.
source: Although less is known about the upstream activator of mTORC2, PtdIns(3,4,5)P3, which is generated by PI3K (Whitman et al., 1988), has been shown to be critical (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: mTORC2 is known to phosphorylate Akt at Serine 473 and increase its kinase activity.
source: mTORC2 is known to phosphorylate Akt at Serine 473 and increase its kinase activity (Guertin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Signaling through IL-15 receptors is obligatory for NK cell development.
source: Signaling through IL-15 receptors is obligatory for NK cell development (DiSanto et al., 1995; Kennedy et al., 2000; Suzuki et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Activation of PI3K is one component of IL-15 receptors signaling.
source: and activation of PI3K is one component of IL-15 receptors signaling (Gu et al., 2000; Zhu et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ncr1iCre-mediated NK-cell-specific ablation of mTOR results in impaired development and effector functions.
source: Indeed, Ncr1iCre-mediated NK-cell-specific ablation of mTOR results in impaired development and effector functions (Marçais et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PDK1, an upstream activator of mTORC1, regulates early NK cell development by inducing Nfil3 which drives the transcription of Eomes.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that PDK1, an upstream activator of mTORC1, regulates early NK cell development by inducing Nfil3 which drives the transcription of Eomes (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: FoxO1, a downstream effector of mTORC2, negatively regulates the terminal maturation of NK cells through direct inhibition of the transcription of Tbx21 (the gene encoding T-bet).
source: FoxO1, a downstream effector of mTORC2, negatively regulates the terminal maturation of NK cells through direct inhibition of the transcription of Tbx21 (the gene encoding T-bet) (Deng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of Raptor protein in NK cells was verified by western blot.
source: Loss of Raptor protein in NK cells was verified by western blot (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The frequency of NK cells was increased in the BM of Rptor cKO compare to WT mice.
source: Phenotypic analyses revealed that the frequency of NK cells was increased in the BM of Rptor cKO compare to WT mice
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Percentages of NK cells in the periphery were significantly reduced in Rptor cKO mice.
source: while percentages of NK cells in the periphery were significantly reduced (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The lymphocytes counts were comparable between WT and Rptor cKO mice in both BM and spleen.
source: The lymphocytes counts were comparable between WT and Rptor cKO mice in both BM and spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The percentage of proliferating NK cells was significantly reduced in Rptor cKO mice at steady-state, as evidenced by Ki-67 staining.
source: The percentage of proliferating NK cells was significantly reduced in Rptor cKO mice at steady-state, as evidenced by Ki-67 staining (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Ki-67 flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The frequency and number of CD45.2+ NK cells were significantly reduced in Rptor cKO mice, indicating impairment in the trafficking of NK cells.
source: The frequency and number of CD45.2+ NK cells were significantly reduced in Rptor cKO mice, indicating impairment in the trafficking of NK cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by CD45.2 staining data shown in Figure 1D and inferred from the experimental design.

claim: There were no differences in cell viability between WT and Rptor cKO NK cells, as demonstrated by Annexin V and Propidium iodide staining.
source: There were no differences in cell viability between WT and Rptor cKO NK cells, as demonstrated by Annexin V and Propidium iodide staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V and PI staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Disruption of mTORC1 impairs homeostatic NK cell proliferation and migration, but not viability.
source: These data showed that disruption of mTORC1 impairs homeostatic NK cell proliferation and migration, but not viability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results (Figures 1C, 1D, and 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Expression of CD122, NK1.1, and DX5 indicated a reduction of the mNK population in the spleen of Rptor cKO mice.
source: Expression of CD122, NK1.1, and DX5 indicated a reduction of the mNK population in the spleen, while the iNK population was similar between WT and Rptor cKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The iNK population was similar between WT and Rptor cKO mice.
source: Expression of CD122, NK1.1, and DX5 indicated a reduction of the mNK population in the spleen, while the iNK population was similar between WT and Rptor cKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No significant changes were observed among NKPs, iNKs, and mNKs in the BM of Rptor cKO mice.
source: No significant changes were observed among NKPs, iNKs, and mNKs in the BM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Raptor deficiency resulted in a significant block in the transition from the CD27 SP to DP stage in both the BM and periphery.
source: Raptor deficiency resulted in a significant block in the transition from the CD27 SP to DP stage in both the BM and periphery (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E and supplementary figures.

claim: The frequency of KLRG1-expressing NK cells was significantly reduced in all organs tested in Rptor cKO mice.
source: Consistent with this, the frequency of KLRG1-expressing NK cells was also significantly reduced in all organs tested (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Analyses of other activating and inhibitory cell surface receptors indicated further developmental defects including reduced expression of Ly49D, Ly49G2, and Ly49H in Rptor cKO mice.
source: Analyses of other activating and inhibitory cell surface receptors indicated further developmental defects including reduced expression of Ly49D, Ly49G2, and Ly49H (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: mTORC1 is required for maintaining NK cell homeostasis through proliferation, migration, and differentiation.
source: Collectively, we conclude that mTORC1 is required for maintaining NK cell homeostasis through proliferation, migration, and differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results presented in Figure 1 and its supplements.

claim: The loss of Rictor protein was verified by western blot.
source: The loss of Rictor protein was verified by western blot (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Loss of mTORC2 did not change frequency or number of NK cells in the BM.
source: Unlike Rptor cKO mice, loss of mTORC2 did not change frequency or number of NK cells in the BM (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The percentages of NK cells were drastically reduced in the periphery of Rictor cKO mice with the exception of inguinal lymph nodes.
source: however, the percentages of NK cells were drastically reduced in the periphery with the exception of inguinal lymph nodes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The absolute numbers of lymphocytes were comparable between WT and Rictor cKO mice in both BM and spleen.
source: The absolute numbers of lymphocytes were comparable between WT and Rictor cKO mice in both BM and spleen (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The frequency of proliferating NK cells at steady-state was significantly reduced in Rictor cKO compare to WT mice.
source: Ki-67 staining indicated the frequency of proliferating NK cells at steady-state was significantly reduced in Rictor cKO compare to WT mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by Ki-67 flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CD45.2 staining revealed a significantly higher number of NK cells in the parenchymal region in Rictor cKO compare to WT mice, implying a potential defect in their migration.
source: Although the total numbers of NK cells in the BM were similar (Figure 2B), CD45.2 staining revealed a significantly higher number of NK cells in the parenchymal region in Rictor cKO compare to WT mice, implying a potential defect in their migration (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by CD45.2 staining data shown in Figure 2D and inferred from the experimental design.

claim: Rictor deficiency did not affect the viability of NK cells.
source: Rictor deficiency did not affect the viability of NK cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V and PI staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of mTORC2 results in defective NK cell proliferation and migration that lead to a reduction of their numbers in the periphery.
source: Together, we conclude that loss of mTORC2 results in defective NK cell proliferation and migration that lead to a reduction of their numbers in the periphery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results (Figures 2C and 2D).

claim: The reduced total NK cell number in the spleen of Rictor cKO mice was exclusively associated with a reduction in the mNK population.
source: The reduced total NK cell number in the spleen of Rictor cKO mice was exclusively associated with a reduction in the mNK population (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There are no significant changes among NKPs, iNKs, and mNKs in the BM of Rictor cKO mice.
source: Similarly, there are no significant changes among NKPs, iNKs, and mNKs in the BM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Loss of Rictor impaired NK cell maturation from the DP stage to CD11b SP stage in both the BM and peripheral organs.
source: Distinct from Rptor cKO mice where NK cell maturation was blocked at the CD27 SP stage, loss of Rictor impaired NK cell maturation from the DP stage to CD11b SP stage in both the BM and peripheral organs (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E and supplementary figures.

claim: This defect in terminal maturation was further validated by a significant reduction in KLRG1-expressing NK cells in all organs tested in Rictor cKO mice.
source: This defect in terminal maturation was further validated by a significant reduction in KLRG1-expressing NK cells in all organs tested (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Loss of Rictor resulted in an altered expression profile of cell surface receptors in NK cells.
source: Loss of Rictor also resulted in an altered expression profile of cell surface receptors in NK cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Expression of activating or inhibitory Ly49 receptors was reduced in Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: Expression of activating or inhibitory Ly49 receptors was reduced, while NK1.1 and DX5 expression were increased on Rictor cKO NK cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: NK1.1 and DX5 expression were increased on Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: Expression of activating or inhibitory Ly49 receptors was reduced, while NK1.1 and DX5 expression were increased on Rictor cKO NK cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: mTORC2 is required for the terminal maturation of NK cells, and therefore regulates NK cell development at a different stage than that of mTORC1.
source: We conclude that mTORC2 is required for the terminal maturation of NK cells, and therefore regulates NK cell development at a different stage than that of mTORC1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the developmental defects in Rptor vs Rictor cKO mice.

claim: Accumulation of CD27 SP NK cells in Rptor cKO mice was similar to earlier findings in Eomesfl/fl VavCre mice or Eomes-negative NK cells that naturally occur in the liver of WT mice.
source: Accumulation of CD27 SP NK cells in Rptor cKO mice (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E) was similar to earlier findings in Eomesfl/fl VavCre mice or Eomes-negative NK cells that naturally occur in the liver of WT mice (Gordon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the current data with prior published findings.

claim: Intracellular staining revealed a significant reduction in the protein levels of Eomes in CD27 SP, DP and CD11b SP NK cells from Rptor cKO mice.
source: Intracellular staining revealed a significant reduction in the protein levels of Eomes in CD27 SP, DP and CD11b SP NK cells from Rptor cKO mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The expression of T-bet was minimal in NK cells within the BM.
source: Compare to Eomes, the expression of T-bet was minimal in NK cells within the BM (Figure 3B) that was consistent with earlier reports (Daussy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B and a citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of Raptor resulted in a moderate reduction in T-bet protein level in NK cells from the spleen.
source: Loss of Raptor resulted in a moderate reduction in T-bet protein level in NK cells from the spleen (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The normal developmental progression from the CD27 SP to DP stage correlated with unaltered expression of Eomes in Rictor-deficient NK cells.
source: On the other hand, the normal developmental progression from the CD27 SP to DP stage (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E) correlated with unaltered expression of Eomes in Rictor-deficient NK cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing developmental data with Eomes expression data.

claim: The defect in the terminal maturation of NK cells in Rictor cKO mice mimicked the maturation defects seen in Tbx21 KO mice.
source: The defect in the terminal maturation of NK cells in Rictor cKO mice mimicked the maturation defects seen in Tbx21 KO mice (Gordon et al., 2012; Townsend et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the current data with prior published findings.

claim: The expression of T-bet is significantly reduced in NK cells from the spleen of Rictor cKO mice.
source: We found the expression of T-bet indeed is significantly reduced in NK cells from the spleen of Rictor cKO mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Eomes binds to the promoter of Il2rb (gene encoding IL-15/IL-2 receptor β chain, CD122) and activates its expression.
source: Eomes binds to the promoter of Il2rb (gene encoding IL-15/IL-2 receptor β chain, CD122) and activates its expression (Intlekofer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The expression of CD122 was significantly reduced on per cell basis in Rptor cKO compared to WT mice in all three subsets of NK cells from BM and spleen.
source: Flow analyses revealed that the expression of CD122 was significantly reduced on per cell basis in Rptor cKO compared to WT mice in all three subsets of NK cells from BM and spleen (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The expression of another subunit of the IL-15 receptor complex, the common γ chain (CD132), was not altered in Rptor cKO NK cells.
source: The expression of another subunit of the IL-15 receptor complex, the common γ chain (CD132), was not altered in Rptor cKO NK cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The reduction of CD122 expression in Rptor cKO NK cells led to reduced STAT5 phosphorylation following ex vivo IL-15 stimulation.
source: The reduction of CD122 expression in Rptor cKO NK cells also led to reduced STAT5 phosphorylation following ex vivo IL-15 stimulation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow data shown in Figure 4B and inferred from the relationship between CD122 and STAT5 signaling.

claim: Besides mTORC1-mediated signaling, other pathways downstream of IL-15 receptors were sub-optimal in Rptor cKO NK cells, which may also have potentially contributed to the developmental defects.
source: These results indicate that besides mTORC1-mediated signaling, other passways downstream of IL-15 receptors were sub-optimal in Rptor cKO NK cells, which may also have potentially contributed to the developmental defects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in CD122 expression and STAT5 phosphorylation.

claim: Rictor cKO NK cells exhibited only a moderate reduction in CD122 expression.
source: Unlike Rptor cKO NK cells that had significant reduction in CD122 expression (Figure 4A), Rictor cKO NK cells exhibited only a moderate reduction (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The expression of CD132 is not altered in Rictor-deficient NK cells.
source: The expression of CD132 is not altered in Rictor-deficient NK cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: IL-15-mediated STAT5 phosphorylation was intact in Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: In addition, IL-15-mediated STAT5 phosphorylation was intact in Rictor cKO NK cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: mTORC1 activity is reduced during the transition from the DP to CD11b SP stage of WT mice.
source: Previous reports have shown that mTORC1 activity is reduced during the transition from the DP to CD11b SP stage of WT mice (Marçais et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylation of rpS6S240/244 is reduced during the transition from DP to CD11b SP NK cells in WT mice.
source: We validated this observation by comparing phosphorylation of rpS6S240/244 and cell size between these two NK subsets from WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cell size is reduced during the transition from DP to CD11b SP NK cells in WT mice.
source: We validated this observation by comparing phosphorylation of rpS6S240/244 and cell size between these two NK subsets from WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The protein levels of Eomes were reduced during the transition from DP to CD11b SP NK cells in WT mice.
source: Concurrently, we found that the protein levels of Eomes were also reduced during this transition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CD122 expression is reduced in the CD11b SP compare to the DP NK cells from WT mice.
source: We also observed a similar reduction in CD122 expression in the CD11b SP compare to the DP NK cells from WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: These phenotypical changes during the transition from the DP to CD11b SP stage of WT mice mimic Raptor-deficient NK cells.
source: These phenotypical changes during the transition from the DP to CD11b SP stage of WT mice mimic Raptor-deficient NK cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the phenotypes of WT NK cells at different stages with Raptor-deficient NK cells.

claim: There is a regulation loop among mTORC1 → Eomes → CD122 → mTORC1 that regulate the development of normal NK cells.
source: This implies a regulation loop among mTORC1 → Eomes → CD122 → mTORC1 that regulate the development of normal NK cells.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed relationships between these factors.

claim: T-bet has been shown to regulate CD122 expression in T cells.
source: Similar to Eomes, T-bet has also been shown to regulate CD122 expression in T cells (Intlekofer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Eomes, but not T-bet, plays a critical role in maintaining CD122 expression in NK cells.
source: which was consistent with the notion that Eomes, but not T-bet, plays a critical role in maintaining CD122 expression in NK cells (Intlekofer et al., 2005; Townsend et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and the observed differences in CD122 expression between Rptor and Rictor cKO NK cells.

claim: 2963 genes in Rptor cKO NK cells were differentially expressed (FDR < 0.05) compared to WT.
source: Compared to their corresponding WT, 2963 genes in Rptor cKO NK cells and 829 genes in Rictor cKO NK cells were differentially expressed (DE; FDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 829 genes in Rictor cKO NK cells were differentially expressed (FDR < 0.05) compared to WT.
source: Compared to their corresponding WT, 2963 genes in Rptor cKO NK cells and 829 genes in Rictor cKO NK cells were differentially expressed (DE; FDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 406 DE genes were overlapped between Rptor and Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: Of which 406 DE genes were overlapped between Rptor and Rictor cKO NK cells, indicating a more profound transcriptomic alteration in Rptor cKO NK cells compared to Rictor cKO NK cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There is a more profound transcriptomic alteration in Rptor cKO NK cells compared to Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: Of which 406 DE genes were overlapped between Rptor and Rictor cKO NK cells, indicating a more profound transcriptomic alteration in Rptor cKO NK cells compared to Rictor cKO NK cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the number of differentially expressed genes in each condition.

claim: The top three significantly enriched signaling pathways in Rptor cKO NK cells are eIF2, eIF4/P70S6K, and mTOR signaling.
source: As downstream targets of mTORC1, the top three significantly enriched signaling pathways in Rptor cKO NK cells are eIF2, eIF4/P70S6K, and mTOR signaling (p=5.53 × 10−23, 2.15 × 10−14, and 4 × 10−14, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by IPA analyses of RNAseq data.

claim: The Z-scores of eIF2, eIF4/P70S6K, and mTOR signaling pathways are positive in Rptor cKO NK cells, which indicates higher translational activity.
source: Unexpectedly, the Z-scores of those three pathways are positive (Z-score = 3.833, 0.894, and 0.73, respectively), which indicates higher translational activity in Rptor cKO NK cells.
evidence: This is supported by IPA analyses of RNAseq data.

claim: Raptor deficiency results in increased transcription of genes encoding proteins that comprise the translation machinery such as eIFs, eEFs and ribosome proteins.
source: After a thorough examination of the molecular signature of those three enriched pathways, we found that Raptor deficiency results in increased transcription of genes encoding proteins that comprise the translation machinery such as eIFs, eEFs and ribosome proteins (Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Compensatory pathways are initiated in Rptor cKO NK cells to overcome the impaired protein translation.
source: This not only explains the positive Z-scores of those three pathways but also reveals that compensatory pathways are initiated in Rptor cKO NK cells to overcome the impaired protein translation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in translation machinery gene expression despite loss of mTORC1.

claim: IPA analyses demonstrated impaired oxidative phosphorylation pathway in Rptor cKO NK cells, indicating defects in mitochondrial functions.
source: IPA analyses also demonstrated impaired oxidative phosphorylation pathway in Rptor cKO NK cells, indicating defects in mitochondrial functions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by IPA analyses of RNAseq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is more than 10-fold induction of Ppargc1a in Rptor cKO NK cells.
source: This coincides with more than 10-fold induction of Ppargc1a in Rptor cKO NK cells (Figure 5B), which is known to be induced under mitochondrial stress conditions (Finck and Kelly, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5B and a citation to prior work.

claim: Ppargc1a is known to be induced under mitochondrial stress conditions.
source: This coincides with more than 10-fold induction of Ppargc1a in Rptor cKO NK cells (Figure 5B), which is known to be induced under mitochondrial stress conditions (Finck and Kelly, 2006).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Integrin signaling is defective in Rptor cKO NK cells.
source: Besides oxidative phosphorylation, integrin signaling is also defective in Rptor cKO NK cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by IPA analyses of RNAseq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The PTEN signaling pathway is impaired in Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: As for Rictor cKO NK cells, the PTEN signaling pathway is impaired (p=1.73 × 10−5, Z-score = −1.069) as demonstrated by increased expression of receptors (Insr, Igf1r) involving growth factors signaling or proteins (Pik3cd, Pik3r5) comprising PI(3)K and decreased expression of phosphatase (Inpp5b) that dampen the inositol phosphates signaling (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by IPA analyses of RNAseq data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There is a potential positive regulation of PTEN by mTORC2 to balance the PI(3,4,5)P3-mediated activation of mTORC2.
source: This indicates that there is a potential positive regulation of PTEN by mTORC2 to balance the PI(3,4,5)P3-mediated activation of mTORC2 (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed PTEN signaling changes and a citation to prior work.

claim: The expression of transcription factors such as Nfil3, Id2, and Eomes that are critical for NK cell commitment and early development are reduced in Rptor but not in Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: The expression of transcription factors such as Nfil3, Id2, and Eomes that are critical for NK cell commitment and early development are reduced in Rptor but not in Rictor cKO NK cells (Table 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Table 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The expression of T-bet and Zeb2 which promote terminal mature NK cell development were significantly reduced in Rictor cKO mice.
source: The expression of T-bet and Zeb2 which promote terminal mature NK cell development were significantly reduced in Rictor cKO mice (Table 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Table 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: This expression pattern correlates with early NK cell development impairment in Rptor cKO mice versus terminal maturation defect seen in Rictor cKO mice.
source: This expression pattern correlates with early NK cell development impairment in Rptor cKO mice versus terminal maturation defect seen in Rictor cKO mice (Figures 1E and 2E).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing transcription factor expression with developmental phenotypes.

claim: Ncr1iCre-mediated deletion of Nfil3 does not alter the development of NK cells.
source: Although Nfil3 has been proposed to induce Id2 and Eomes (Male et al., 2014), Ncr1iCre-mediated deletion of Nfil3 does not alter the development of NK cells (Firth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Id2 is critical to suppress the expression of E-protein target genes during NK cell development.
source: Delconte et al. have shown that Id2 is critical to suppress the expression of E-protein target genes during NK cell development.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: There is no induction of E-protein target genes in Rptor cKO NK cells.
source: However, we did not find induction of those E-protein target genes in Rptor cKO NK cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis.

claim: There is a significant enrichment of Eomes target genes in Rptor cKO NK cells.
source: On the contrary, compared with the WT controls, we found a significant enrichment of Eomes target genes in Rptor cKO NK cells (p=6.11 × 10−3, Z-score = −0.988) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by IPA analyses of RNAseq data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The deficiency of Eomes in Rptor cKO NK cells is more likely to be responsible for the developmental defects.
source: This indicates that the deficiency of Eomes in Rptor cKO NK cells is more likely to be responsible for the developmental defects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of Eomes target genes and lack of E-protein target gene induction.

claim: Both Raptor and Rictor deficiency results in reduced transcripts level of S1pr5.
source: In addition, we identified that both Raptor and Rictor deficiency results in reduced transcripts level of S1pr5 (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The reduced S1pr5 expression further implies the migration defects of both Raptor- and Rictor-deficient NK cells.
source: This further implies the migration defects of both Raptor- and Rictor-deficient NK cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of S1pr5 in cell migration.

claim: An increase in the transcript level of Socs2 in Rictor cKO NK cells may contribute to their impaired proliferation and reduced cellularity.
source: Moreover, an increase in the transcript level of Socs2 in Rictor cKO NK cells (Figure 5C) may contribute to their impaired proliferation and reduced cellularity (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on RNAseq data and a citation to prior work on Socs2 function.

claim: Rictor, but not Raptor, deficiency results in reduced transcripts level of Ifng and Gzmb.
source: Related to NK cell effector functions, the RNA sequencing data revealed that Rictor, but not Raptor, deficiency results in reduced transcripts level of Ifng and Gzmb (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The mRNA level of Granzyme B is significantly increased in Rptor cKO NK cells.
source: In fact, the mRNA level of Granzyme B is significantly increased in Rptor cKO NK cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Loss of Raptor or Rictor impaired the expression of Ccl3 and Ccl4.
source: Loss of Raptor or Rictor impaired the expression of Ccl3 and Ccl4 (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: There is a significant enrichment of T-bet target genes in Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: Consistent with reduced T-bet expression in mRNA (Table 1) and protein level (Figure 3D), we found a significant enrichment of T-bet target genes (p=4.59 × 10−14, Z-score = −1.429) in Rictor cKO NK cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by IPA analyses of RNAseq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The well-established T-bet-induced genes (Klrg1, Ifng, Gzmb, S1pr5, Zeb2) were reduced in Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: The well-established T-bet-induced genes (Klrg1, Ifng, Gzmb, S1pr5, Zeb2) (Simonetta et al., 2016) were reduced in Rictor cKO NK cells (Figures 6A and 5C).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figures 6A and 5C and a citation to prior work.

claim: mTORC2 phosphorylates Serine473 on Akt, which is critical for Akt to phosphorylate FoxO transcription factors.
source: Earlier work showed that mTORC2 phosphorylates Serine473 on Akt, which is critical for Akt to phosphorylate FoxO transcription factors (Brunet et al., 1999; Guertin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: After Akt-mediated phosphorylation, modulator protein 14-3-3 binds to FoxO transcription factors and reduces their transcriptional activity by blocking DNA binding and accelerating nuclear exportation.
source: After Akt-mediated phosphorylation, modulator protein 14-3-3 binds to FoxO transcription factors and reduces their transcriptional activity by blocking DNA binding and accelerating nuclear exportation (Brunet et al., 1999; Cahill et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: FoxO1 is the most abundant FoxO family member expressed in NK cells.
source: Among the FoxO families, FoxO1 is the most abundant one expressed in NK cells and has been shown to negatively regulate the terminal maturation of NK cells by suppressing the transcription of Tbx21 (Deng et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: FoxO1 has been shown to negatively regulate the terminal maturation of NK cells by suppressing the transcription of Tbx21.
source: Among the FoxO families, FoxO1 is the most abundant one expressed in NK cells and has been shown to negatively regulate the terminal maturation of NK cells by suppressing the transcription of Tbx21 (Deng et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Lack of Rictor resulted in a reduced level of AktS473 phosphorylation in the NK cells from BM.
source: Lack of Rictor resulted in a reduced level of AktS473 phosphorylation in the NK cells from BM (Figure 6B, top).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Reduced phosphorylation of FoxO1T24 was detected in Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: Consistent with this, we also detected reduced phosphorylation of FoxO1T24 in these Rictor cKO NK cells (Figure 6B, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The transcriptional activity of FoxO1 is higher in Rictor cKO compared to WT NK cells.
source: These data suggested that the transcriptional activity of FoxO1 is higher in Rictor cKO compared to WT NK cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced phosphorylation of FoxO1.

claim: There is a significant enrichment of FoxO1 target genes in Rictor cKO NK cells compared with WT in the IPA analyses.
source: Indeed, we found a significant enrichment of FoxO1 target genes (p=4.46 × 10–9, Z-score = 1.719) in Rictor cKO NK cells compared with WT in the IPA analyses (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by IPA analyses of RNAseq data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Fisher's exact test showed enrichment of the FoxO1-target genes with p-value equal to 1.32 × 10−10 in Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: Consistent with the IPA analyses, our Fisher's exact test showed enrichment of the FoxO1-target genes with p-value equal to 1.32 × 10−10, emphasizing a hyperactive FoxO1 in the Rictor cKO NK cells.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of RNAseq data.

claim: There is reduced mRNA level of Tbx21 in CD27+ NK cell subset from both BM and spleen of Rictor cKO mice.
source: Consistent with the RNA sequencing data, we found reduced mRNA level of Tbx21 in CD27+ NK cell subset from both BM and spleen of Rictor cKO mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There is significantly elevated mRNA level of known FoxO1 activated genes including Bcl2, Klf2, Il7r and Ccr7 in the CD27+ Rictor cKO NK cells compared to the WT.
source: We also found significantly elevated mRNA level of known FoxO1 activated genes including Bcl2, Klf2, Il7r and Ccr7 in the CD27+ Rictor cKO NK cells compared to the WT (Figure 6D) (Kerdiles et al., 2009; Ouyang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D and citations to prior work.

claim: There is higher cell surface expression of IL-7Rα and Ccr7 in Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: This is also consistent with higher cell surface expression of IL-7Rα and Ccr7 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The impaired mTORC2-AktS473-FoxO1 signaling axis results in hyperactive FoxO1 that potentially suppresses the expression of T-bet in Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: Based on these, we conclude that the impaired mTORC2-AktS473-FoxO1 signaling axis results in hyperactive FoxO1 that potentially suppresses the expression of T-bet in Rictor cKO NK cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing reduced AktS473 and FoxO1 phosphorylation, enrichment of FoxO1 target genes, and reduced T-bet expression.

claim: Phosphorylation of rpS6 is nearly abolished in Raptor-deficient NK cells.
source: Being downstream of mTORC1, phosphorylation of rpS6 is nearly abolished in Raptor-deficient NK cells, as expected (Figure 7A, left).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Deficiency of mTORC2 does not perturb mTORC1 signaling as phosphorylation of rpS6 is moderately increased in Rictor cKO compared to WT NK cells.
source: Important, deficiency of mTORC2 does not perturb mTORC1 signaling as phosphorylation of rpS6 is moderately increased in Rictor cKO compared to WT NK cells (Figure 7A, right).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The moderate augmentation in mTORC1 activity could potentially result from reduced PTEN signaling as indicated by the RNA sequencing data.
source: The moderate augmentation in mTORC1 activity could potentially result from reduced PTEN signaling as indicated by the RNA sequencing data (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in mTORC1 activity and the RNAseq data showing impaired PTEN signaling.

claim: There is a moderate decrease in mTORC2 activity indicated by phosphorylation of AktS473 in Rptor cKO NK cells stimulated with IL-15.
source: On the other hand, we did observe a moderate decrease in mTORC2 activity indicated by phosphorylation of AktS473 in Rptor cKO NK cells stimulated with IL-15 (Figure 7B, left).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The moderate decrease in mTORC2 activity in Rptor cKO NK cells is potentially due to reduced expression of IL-15/IL-2 receptor β chain (CD122).
source: This is potentially due to reduced expression of IL-15/IL-2 receptor β chain (CD122) as the phosphorylation of STAT5 is also moderately reduced in Rptor cKO NK cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in CD122 expression and STAT5 phosphorylation.

claim: AktS473 phosphorylation was abolished in Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: As expected, AktS473 phosphorylation was abolished in Rictor cKO NK cells (Figure 7B, right).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Disruption of mTORC2 does not affect IL-15-mediated mTORC1 activation in NK cells.
source: Based on these, we conclude that disruption of mTORC2 does not affect IL-15-mediated mTORC1 activation in NK cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phospho-flow data showing intact rpS6 phosphorylation in Rictor cKO NK cells.

claim: The tumor metastases were much more severe in the lungs of Rptor or Rictor cKO mice compared to corresponding WT control mice.
source: Compared to corresponding WT control mice, the tumor metastases were much more severe in the lungs of Rptor or Rictor cKO mice (Figure 8A − D).
evidence: This is supported by tumor burden data shown in Figure 8A-D.

claim: The significant reduction of NK cell number and the terminal mature NK cells in both of the cKO mice might contribute to the defective antitumor response.
source: The significant reduction of NK cell number and the terminal mature NK cells in both of the cKO mice might contribute to this defective antitumor response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed NK cell defects and tumor burden.

claim: The clearance efficiency of the transferred β2-microglobulin-deficient targets cells was significantly impaired in Rptor or Rictor cKO mice.
source: Similar to the B16F10 tumor challenge, the clearance efficiency of the transferred β2-microglobulin-deficient targets cells was significantly impaired in Rptor or Rictor cKO mice (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo rejection assay data shown in Figure 8E and F.

claim: The NK-cell-mediated anti-tumor response is defective in Rptor or Rictor cKO mice.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrated that the NK-cell-mediated anti-tumor response is defective in Rptor or Rictor cKO mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tumor challenge and rejection assay data.

claim: Raptor-deficient NK cells had significantly reduced degranulation when stimulated by RMA/s cells.
source: Compared to WT control, Raptor-deficient NK cells had significantly reduced degranulation, and almost abolished IFN-γ production when stimulated by RMA/s cells (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: Raptor-deficient NK cells had almost abolished IFN-γ production when stimulated by RMA/s cells.
source: Compared to WT control, Raptor-deficient NK cells had significantly reduced degranulation, and almost abolished IFN-γ production when stimulated by RMA/s cells (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: mTORC1 is not required for IL-12/IL-18-mediated IFN-γ production.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Marçais et al., 2014), mTORC1 is not required for IL-12/IL-18-mediated IFN-γ production (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9A and B and a citation to prior work.

claim: Impaired effector functions of Raptor-deficient NK cells were observed when stimulated with PMA/Ionomycin.
source: We also observed impaired effector functions of Raptor-deficient NK cells when stimulated with PMA/Ionomycin (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: The effector functions of Rictor cKO NK cells are intact regardless of the type of stimuli.
source: In contrast, the effector functions of Rictor cKO NK cells are intact regardless of the type of stimuli (Figure 9C and D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9C and D.

claim: Raptor-deficient NK cells expand poorly in IL-2 culture.
source: Consistent with the critical role of mTORC1 downstream of IL-2 in regulating cell growth and proliferation, the Raptor-deficient NK cells expand poorly in culture.
evidence: This is an observation from in vitro culture experiments.

claim: Rictor-deficient NK cells respond to IL-2 and expand normally as their WT control.
source: Rictor-deficient NK cells respond to IL-2 and expand normally as their WT control, consistent with relatively optimal CD122 expression and STAT5 signaling (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is an observation from in vitro culture experiments and is consistent with prior data.

claim: Neither inhibition of mTORC1 by Rapamycin nor Rictor deficiency resulted in changes in the ability of NK cells to lyse the sensitive targets.
source: Neither inhibition of mTORC1 by Rapamycin nor Rictor deficiency resulted in changes in the ability of NK cells to lyse the sensitive targets (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating that both mTOR complexes are dispensable for the conjugate formation and delivery of cytolytic vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by 51Cr-release assay data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Both mTOR complexes are dispensable for the conjugate formation and delivery of cytolytic vesicles.
source: Neither inhibition of mTORC1 by Rapamycin nor Rictor deficiency resulted in changes in the ability of NK cells to lyse the sensitive targets (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating that both mTOR complexes are dispensable for the conjugate formation and delivery of cytolytic vesicles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cytotoxicity assay data.

claim: The degranulation defects seen in the in vivo Poly (I:C)-activated Raptor-deficient NK cells potentially results from the reduced storage of cytolytic granules as mTORC1 is critical in cytokines-mediated priming of NK cells.
source: The degranulation defects seen in the in vivo Poly (I:C)-activated Raptor-deficient NK cells (Figure 9A and B) potentially results from the reduced storage of cytolytic granules as mTORC1 is critical in cytokines-mediated priming of NK cells (Marçais et al., 2014; Nandagopal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed degranulation defects and citations to prior work.

claim: Rapamycin inhibits the production of IFN-γ downstream of activating receptor NKG2D, but not PMA/Ionomycin.
source: As for cytokine generation, Rapamycin inhibits the production of IFN-γ downstream of activating receptor NKG2D, but not PMA/Ionomycin (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IL-2-activated Rictor-deficient NK cells produce IFN-γ comparable to the WT control.
source: Consistent with the ex vivo functional assay (Figure 9C and D), IL-2-activated Rictor-deficient NK cells produce IFN-γ comparable to the WT control (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1D.

claim: mTORC1, but not mTORC2, is critical to the effector functions of NK cells.
source: In summary, these data demonstrate that mTORC1, but not mTORC2, is critical to the effector functions of NK cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple functional assays comparing Rptor and Rictor cKO NK cells.

claim: Ncr1iCre-mediated deletion of mTOR results in an impairment in the transition of CD27 SP to DP and defective IL-15-mediated STAT5 activation.
source: In NK cells, the earlier study revealed the essential role of mTOR in controlling development following Ncr1 expression (Marçais et al., 2014). This study revealed that lack of mTOR resulted in an impairment in the transition of CD27 SP to DP and defective IL-15-mediated STAT5 activation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: It is impossible to elucidate the precise molecular mechanisms by which mTOR regulate distinct developmental progression of NK cells with the concurrent loss of both mTORC1 and mTORC2.
source: Moreover, it is impossible to elucidate the precise molecular mechanisms by which mTOR regulate distinct developmental progression of NK cells with the concurrent loss of both mTORC1 and mTORC2.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the limitations of studying total mTOR deletion.

claim: The independent disruption of mTORC1 or mTORC2 results in defective NK cell maturation at distinct developmental stages.
source: Phenotypic analyses revealed that both mTOR complexes are critical for the homeostasis of NK cells and that the independent disruption of mTORC1 or mTORC2 results in defective NK cell maturation at distinct developmental stages.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the phenotypic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The differential alteration of the expression of Eomes and T-bet in Rptor or Rictor cKO mice provide a potential mechanistic explanation for the maturation defects.
source: The differential alteration of the expression of Eomes and T-bet in Rptor or Rictor cKO mice provide a potential mechanistic explanation for the maturation defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transcription factor expression data.

claim: Neither Rptor nor Rictor cKO mice demonstrated robust NK cell-mediated antitumor responses.
source: In the physiological context, neither Rptor nor Rictor cKO mice demonstrated robust NK cell-mediated antitumor responses, highlighting the biological consequences of lacking either mTORC1 or mTORC2.
evidence: This is supported by the tumor challenge and rejection assay data.

claim: Ncr1Cre-mediated deletion of Pdpk1 or Tsc1 did not have any impact on NK cell development.
source: Despite our findings using Rptor cKO mice, Ncr1Cre-mediated deletion of Pdpk1 or Tsc1 did not have any impact on NK cell development (Yang et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Following Ncr1 expression, mTORC1 is potentially activated through an alternative mechanism instead of the canonical PI3K-PDK1-Akt-TSC1/2-mTORC1 pathway.
source: This suggests that following Ncr1 expression, mTORC1 is potentially activated through an alternative mechanism instead of the canonical PI3K-PDK1-Akt-TSC1/2-mTORC1 pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the current findings with prior genetic deletion studies.

claim: mTORC1 is also likely critical for early NK cell commitment and development at pre-Ncr1 stages based on the phenotype seen in Pdpk1fl/fl Vav1Cre mice.
source: In addition, mTORC1 is also likely critical for early NK cell commitment and development at pre-Ncr1 stages based on the phenotype seen in Pdpk1fl/fl Vav1Cre mice (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on a citation to prior work.

claim: Selective disruption of mTORC1 leads to increased transcripts level of eIFs, eEFs, and ribosomal proteins, implying an alternative pathway that compensates the protein translation defects.
source: However, less is known about the regulation of these proteins at the transcriptional level, especially related to the loss of mTORC1. In this context, our RNAseq analyses revealed that selective disruption of mTORC1 leads to increased transcripts level of eIFs, eEFs, and ribosomal proteins, implying an alternative pathway that compensates the protein translation defects.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNAseq data.

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation and integrin signaling are impaired in Rptor cKO NK cells.
source: Gene ontology analyses also revealed that oxidative phosphorylation and integrin signaling are impaired in Rptor cKO NK cells.
evidence: This is supported by IPA analyses of RNAseq data.

claim: These findings related to oxidative phosphorylation and integrin signaling are novel and have not been implicated with mTORC1 in lymphocytes.
source: These findings are novel and have not been implicated with mTORC1 in lymphocytes.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Among Nfil3, Id2, and Eomes, the reduced Eomes expression is more likely responsible for the maturation defects due to the exclusive loss of mTORC1.
source: This indicates that among those three transcription factors, the reduced Eomes expression is more likely responsible for the maturation defects due to the exclusive loss of mTORC1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of Eomes target genes and lack of E-protein target gene induction.

claim: During NK cell development, stimuli (presumably IL-15) activate mTORC2-AktS473-FoxO1 signaling cascade that reveals the suppression of T-bet from FoxO1.
source: While this pathway has previously been shown to control CD8 T cell memory differentiation (Pollizzi et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016), our work establishes that during NK cell development, stimuli (presumably IL-15) activate mTORC2-AktS473-FoxO1 signaling cascade that reveals the suppression of T-bet from FoxO1
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and citations to prior work in T cells.

claim: The mTORC2-AktS473-FoxO1 signaling axis is indispensable to maintain NK cell homeostasis and drive terminal maturation.
source: and this signaling axis is indispensable to maintain NK cell homeostasis and drive terminal maturation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing the effects of Rictor deletion.

claim: PTEN signaling is impaired in Rictor cKO NK cells, which indicates a balanced activation loop consists of PI(3)K-PI(3,4,5)P3-mTORC2-PTEN.
source: The RNAseq analyses also revealed that PTEN signaling is impaired in Rictor cKO NK cells, which indicates a balanced activation loop consists of PI(3)K-PI(3,4,5)P3-mTORC2-PTEN.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNAseq data.

claim: The impaired PTEN signaling may contribute to the moderately increased mTORC1 activity in Rictor cKO NK cells.
source: This may contribute to the moderately increased mTORC1 activity in Rictor cKO NK cells.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed PTEN signaling changes and mTORC1 activity.

claim: The overall effector functions are normal in Poly (I:C)-primed or IL-2-cultured Rictor-deficient NK cells.
source: The overall effector functions are normal in Poly (I:C)-primed or IL-2-cultured Rictor-deficient NK cells.
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 9C and D and supplementary figures.

claim: Careful considerations should be taken when utilizing mTOR inhibitors following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation since manipulation of mTOR complexes can potentially compromise NK cell development and repopulation.
source: Our study implies that careful considerations should be taken when utilizing mTOR inhibitors following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation since manipulation of mTOR complexes can potentially compromise NK cell development and repopulation.
evidence: This is a speculative implication based on the study findings.
